Theme

Body, health & movement

lip noun

also lips, lower lip, upper lip

classical

Caes. BG 5.14: labrum superius
Plin. NH 9.64: īnferiōrī labrō
Traupman 58, 340

1labrum: short a (Lewis & Short lā̆brum, common). Hor. C. 1.13.12, dente labrīs notam, the close of a lesser asclepiad: la- takes a short place; Vergil makes the syllable heavy before br (E. 3.43, necdum illīs labra admōvī). De Vaan 319, s.v. labium. Lābrum, a basin, is another word, from lavābrum (de Vaan 330).

labrum1, labrī n.

noun, second declension

The ordinary word. Labrum superius, the upper lip; labrum īnferius, the lower (Traupman). Not lābrum, a basin.

Other words

  • labellum, labellī n. — little lip; a baby’s lips

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Div. 1.78; Catull. 61.209–213

    The diminutive, of a baby’s lips; in Plautus a pet name too (Lewis & Short).

  • labium, labiī n. — lip; mostly in the plural, labia

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Plin. NH 29.46 (Lewis & Short); Vulg. Ps. 50 (51), 17

    Ante- and post-classical for labrum (Lewis & Short): Plautus’s and Terence’s feminine labea, Pliny’s neuter plural labia, and so in Church Latin.

Examples

  • Torquātus volō parvulus mātris ē gremiō suae porrigēns tenerās manūs dulce rīdeat ad patrem sēmihiante labellō

    I want a little Torquatus, reaching out his tender hands from his mother’s lap, to laugh sweetly at his father with half-open lipsCatull. 61.209–213

  • Platōnī cum in cūnīs parvulō dormientī apēs in labellīs cōnsēdissent

    when Plato was a baby asleep in his cradle and bees settled on his little lipsCic. Div. 1.78

  • Domine, labia mea aperiēs, et ōs meum annūntiābit laudem tuam.

    Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.Vulg. Ps. 50 (51), 17

See also mouth, kiss, put a finger to one’s lips.
